title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 95–96
description: Formal and informal vocabulary, official forms, CV sections, job-application terminology and practical writing advice, with register-sensitive original examples.

units.title: Unit 95 — Formal and informal English
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 196–197 (PDF pages 197–198).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Language register in public notices, announcements, correspondence and conversation
learningObjectives: Recognise formal words used in notices, official correspondence and public announcements.
Select neutral equivalents for formal verbs and phrases such as purchase, commence, depart and proceed to.
Use informal spoken words and phrases appropriately among friends, including mate, cheers, bloke and make it.
Recognise the meanings and limitations of informal language such as stuff, dying for and a load of rubbish.
Rewrite messages at an appropriate level of formality and recognise dictionary labels for register.

items.example: The announcement used formal English to address passengers.
items.note: This register is common in notices, official letters, speeches and announcements.

items.example: Visitors can purchase tickets at the information desk.
items.note: Formal or business-style alternative to buy.

items.example: You can buy your ticket online before the event.
items.note: Everyday equivalent of the more formal verb purchase.

items.pt: no local; nas instalações do estabelecimento
items.example: Food bought elsewhere must not be eaten on the premises.
items.note: Formal phrase meaning inside a particular building or business property.

items.example: We regret to inform you that your booking has been cancelled.
items.note: Formal way to introduce disappointing or negative news; generally followed by that + clause.

items.pt: não poder; não ser capaz de
items.example: Unfortunately, we are unable to process the request today.
items.note: Polite or formal alternative to cannot; follow with the base verb.

items.example: If you require assistance, please ask a member of staff.
items.note: Often more formal than need, especially in written instructions.

items.example: For further assistance, contact our support team.
items.note: Formal phrase commonly seen in written customer-service messages.

items.pt: por favor, entre em contato com
items.example: Please contact the office if your address changes.
items.note: A standard polite instruction in notices and formal correspondence.

items.example: Send the completed document to the above address.
items.note: Written reference to an address already given earlier on a page or form.

items.example: The council may grant permission for the building work.
items.note: A formal verb meaning officially give or allow something; often grant a request, visa or permission.

items.word: not be in a position to
items.pt: não estar em condições de; não poder
items.example: We are not in a position to approve further applications.
items.note: A diplomatic formal expression used when an organisation cannot take a requested action.

items.example: I am writing regarding your recent enquiry.
items.note: A formal preposition similar to about.

items.example: The ceremony will commence at eleven o’clock.
items.note: Formal alternative to start or begin, especially in public announcements.

items.example: The coach will depart from the main entrance at noon.
items.note: A more formal way of saying leave, often used for journeys and transport.

items.example: Passengers should proceed to the departure lounge.
items.note: A formal direction meaning go to a place; common in airports and public announcements.

items.example: The museum does not permit photography in this gallery.
items.note: Formal alternative to allow; permit something or permit someone to do something.

items.example: Written permission is required to enter this area.
items.note: A related noun useful with grant and permit in formal communication.

items.example: Informal English is common when friends talk to each other.
items.note: Often appropriate in casual conversation and personal messages but less suitable for official correspondence.

items.example: A mate from college invited me to a concert.
items.note: Informal British English for a friend.

items.pt: bastante; com frequência; uma boa quantidade
items.example: I see my old neighbours quite a bit.
items.note: In this conversation, the phrase means fairly often; it can also express a significant amount.

items.example: The bloke who repaired my bicycle was very friendly.
items.note: Informal British English for a man; not suitable for most formal writing.

items.example: I cannot make it to the meeting on Thursday.
items.note: In this sense, make it means manage to come or attend, not manufacture something.

items.example: You cannot join us this weekend? That’s a shame.
items.note: An informal or neutral way to express disappointment or sympathy.

items.pt: a questão é que; acontece que
items.example: I would come, but the thing is, I have to work late.
items.note: Spoken introduction to the real explanation or problem.

items.example: The kids are playing in the garden.
items.note: Informal alternative to children.

items.example: We expect twenty people or so at the party.
items.note: Placed after a number or quantity to mean approximately.

items.pt: telefonar para alguém; ligar para alguém
items.example: I will ring my sister when I get home.
items.note: Common British English for telephone someone; informal or neutral.

items.example: Cheers for helping me carry the boxes.
items.note: Informal British English meaning thanks; cheers can also be a toast.

items.pt: aposto que; tenho certeza de que
items.example: I bet you are excited about your new job.
items.note: A conversational way to say I am sure or I strongly expect something.

items.pt: estar louco por algo; querer muito algo
items.example: After the long walk, we were dying for a cold drink.
items.note: An informal exaggeration meaning want something very much; not literally dying.

items.example: Could you move your stuff away from the door?
items.note: An uncountable informal noun referring to unspecified things or materials; not stuffs in this sense.

items.example: We put all our camping stuff in the car before breakfast.
items.note: Stuff remains uncountable even when it refers to several objects.

items.pt: o que você vai fazer?; o que está aprontando?
items.example: What are you up to after work?
items.note: Informal question about someone’s activities or plans; do not interpret it literally as physical position.

items.example: The new café has great coffee and friendly staff.
items.note: Common informal or neutral praise for something very good.

items.example: We had a terrific afternoon at the beach.
items.note: Enthusiastic informal approval, similar to fantastic or wonderful.

items.example: I thought the article was a load of rubbish.
items.note: Informal and strongly negative: something terrible, poor quality or nonsense.

items.example: Waiting for two hours without a book was a drag.
items.note: Informal expression for something boring or unpleasant.

items.example: That horror film was too scary for the children.
items.note: Informal or everyday alternative to frightening.

items.example: The second-hand coat only cost fifteen quid.
items.note: Informal British English for pounds sterling; quid usually has the same form in the plural.

items.pt: cuidar de alguém; tomar conta de alguém
items.example: My brother will look after the children tonight.
items.note: Common everyday expression for taking care of someone.

sectionsChecked: A: Formal English in café notices, letters, police statements, theatre, stations and airports
B: Informal English across four dialogues; language-help box on uncountable stuff

units.title: Unit 96 — Completing forms and CVs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 198–199 (PDF pages 199–200).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Official forms, personal information, CV sections and job or university applications
learningObjectives: Identify registration, enrolment, entry, landing and visa application forms in the situations described in the textbook.
Understand formal field labels such as date of birth, country of origin and marital status.
Distinguish personal, educational, professional and career-related information on a CV.
Use common job-application expressions such as apply for, qualifications, work experience, references and personal statement.
Apply the textbook’s advice to write a concise, readable, relevant CV or personal statement with correct details.

items.example: Please complete this form before your appointment.
items.note: A document with spaces for required information.

items.pt: formulário de cadastro; formulário de inscrição
items.example: New members complete a registration form at reception.
items.note: A form used to add someone to an official list.

items.pt: formulário de matrícula; de inscrição em curso
items.example: I returned the enrolment form to the language school.
items.note: A form for joining a course or programme; British spelling enrolment.

items.pt: formulário de inscrição (em exame ou competição)
items.example: You must send the exam entry form before the deadline.
items.note: A form used to enter an examination or competition.

items.pt: cartão de desembarque; formulário de entrada no país
items.example: The traveller completed a landing card during the flight.
items.note: A border-entry document used in the book’s example; actual requirements vary by country and date.

items.example: She completed the visa application form online.
items.note: An official form for requesting a visa; application procedures depend on the country.

items.example: They decided to apply for a visa well before their trip.
items.note: Apply for + noun names something requested through an official process.

items.example: Please fill in a form with your contact details.
items.note: Common British English: fill in a form. Fill out a form is also used.

items.pt: preencher um formulário; completar um formulário
items.example: All applicants must complete the form by Friday.
items.note: Formal or neutral alternative to fill in a form.

items.example: Enter your date of birth in the first box.
items.note: Standard form label asking when someone was born.

items.example: Her place of birth is printed on the certificate.
items.note: Form label asking for the town, city or other place where someone was born.

items.example: The application asks for each applicant’s country of origin.
items.note: A formal label relating to the country a person comes from; its precise administrative meaning depends on the form.

items.example: You may be asked to provide your marital status on an official form.
items.note: An administrative category for whether someone is single, married and other recognised statuses.

items.example: Check that your date of arrival is correct on the booking.
items.note: Formal label for when someone arrived or is expected to arrive.

items.pt: data de partida; data de saída
items.example: The hotel asked for our expected date of departure.
items.note: Formal label for when someone leaves or is due to leave.

items.example: The document must be signed before it is sent.
items.note: A form label or instruction indicating that a signature is required.

items.example: Please put your signature at the bottom of the page.
items.note: The special written form of your name used to sign documents.

items.example: Remember to sign the form before returning it.
items.note: Sign is the verb; signature is the noun.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Send your CV with a short covering letter.
items.note: Initialism for curriculum vitae; pronounced as two letter names in British English.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: The employer requested a curriculum vitae in English.
items.note: Full Latin term usually abbreviated to CV.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: The recruiter asked for an updated résumé.
items.note: Used especially in American English for a document summarising experience and qualifications.

items.pt: candidatar-se a uma vaga; solicitar emprego
items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: I plan to apply for a job in software development.
items.note: Apply for + a job or position; the candidate sends an application.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Put your email address under personal details.
items.note: The CV section normally containing identifying and contact information.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: The education section lists her college and university.
items.note: A CV heading for schools, universities or training completed.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: The position requires technical qualifications and practical experience.
items.note: Qualifications can be degrees, certificates and other formally recognised achievements.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: He completed a university degree in biology.
items.note: A qualification awarded after university study.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: My work experience includes two years in customer support.
items.note: A CV section about previous jobs and related professional activities.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Her interests include hiking and playing the guitar.
items.note: A CV section listing relevant or personal activities someone enjoys.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Communication and programming skills are useful in this role.
items.note: Learned or practised abilities that may be relevant to a job or course.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: His career aims include becoming a team leader.
items.note: Statements about what someone hopes to achieve in their working life.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: The company requested a reference from my previous manager.
items.note: A letter or assessment from someone who can comment on a candidate’s suitability.

items.pt: referências profissionais; pessoas que podem recomendar
items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: She provided two references when she applied for the post.
items.note: On a CV this can mean people who can provide recommendations, not just the letters themselves.

items.pt: declaração pessoal; texto de apresentação acadêmica
items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: He wrote a personal statement explaining why he wanted to study medicine.
items.note: An application text describing motivation, educational background and suitability for a course.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Her educational background includes a college diploma and a language course.
items.note: Your previous formal study and training.

items.section: C · A CV and job applications
items.example: Your experience makes you suitable for this position.
items.note: Used to say a candidate, item or choice fits a particular need or purpose.

items.example: A helpful tip is to check your dates carefully.
items.note: A short, useful piece of advice; countable: one tip, two tips.

items.example: Type your application so it is easy to read.
items.note: Here type is a verb meaning produce text using a keyboard, not handwriting.

items.example: Her handwriting is neat, but she submitted a typed CV.
items.note: Writing produced by hand; the textbook recommends typed CVs and statements.

items.example: Keep it simple and make each point easy to understand.
items.note: Practical advice for producing a clear document without unnecessary complexity.

items.example: The application instructions looked complicated at first.
items.note: Describes something with too many difficult or confusing details.

items.pt: verificar se há erros; revisar erros
items.example: Always check for mistakes before sending a CV.
items.note: Proofreading is important before submitting a formal application.

items.example: Make sure the phone number is correct.
items.note: Use make sure + that-clause to express a necessary check or certainty.

items.example: Include only experience that is relevant to the role.
items.note: Relevant information is connected to, and useful for, a particular purpose.

items.example: I often prepare reports on my own.
items.note: Means independently or without the help of others, in this context.

items.example: She enjoys working in a team with other designers.
items.note: A skill involving cooperation with a group of colleagues.

items.pt: carteira de habilitação; habilitação para dirigir
items.example: A driving licence may be useful for jobs that involve travel.
items.note: The textbook exercise treats a driving licence as a potentially useful CV skill or qualification.

items.example: For this exercise, aim for a CV that is no longer than two pages.
items.note: The book recommends this length for CVs; real application requirements can differ.
